section_summary: This section covers U.S. State Department records from 1941 to 1944 concerning the proceedings, reorganization, and legislative actions of the Japanese Imperial Diet during World War II. It details the Diet's 76th, 81st, 83rd, and 85th sessions, focusing on wartime mobilization laws, record budget appropriations, the dissolution of traditional political parties, and controversies surrounding the Imperial Rule Assistance Association. Reports and intelligence analyses from Tokyo, Buenos Aires, Chungking, Moscow, and Washington trace the centralization of executive power under Prime Minister Hideki Tojo and monitor Japan's political and military posture toward Southeast Asia and the Soviet Union.

subfiles.about: Concluding remarks of an official address addressing the Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere, the Three-Power Pact, and honoring the Japanese armed forces.
subfiles.summary: This document represents the concluding text of an official address emphasizing the necessity of ending the current war and establishing a sphere of common prosperity throughout Greater East Asia. The speaker highlights Japan's unbroken imperial line and strategic geographical position as foundational to its world role, expressing confidence in the eventual success of the Three Power Pact. The address concludes with tributes to fallen officers and soldiers and expressions of gratitude to the armed forces serving in the field.
subfiles.title: Address on Greater East Asia and the Three-Power Pact (Conclusion)

subfiles.about: Reports on a secret session of both houses of the Japanese Diet regarding the Thailand-Indochina mediation, international situation, and the China incident.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew reports that both houses of the Imperial Diet convened in secret session on March 15, 1941. Members heard reports from the Prime Minister, Foreign Minister, Army Minister, and Navy Minister. The presentations covered the Thailand-Indochina mediation, the general international situation, and the ongoing progress of the China incident.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 413: Diet Secret Session on Thailand-Indochina Mediation and China Incident

subfiles.about: Reports the formal close of the 76th Diet session, summarizing legislative accomplishments and domestic press criticism regarding party politics and foreign opportunities.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports that the 76th session of the Imperial Diet closed on March 26, 1941, having approved a budget exceeding 13 billion yen and passed 87 bills, including revisions to the National General Mobilization Law and National Defense Security Law. Editorial commentary from newspapers including Miyako and Yomiuri praised the legislative speed but criticized persistent party loyalties, inadequate interpellations, and friction over the Imperial Rule Assistance Association. Press commentary also highlighted the international situation as a unique opportunity to secure essential raw materials and resolve issues in the Netherlands East Indies while the United States was preoccupied with aiding England.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 464: Closing of the 76th Diet Session and Press Comment

subfiles.about: Summarizes Tokyo Despatch No. 5496 regarding procedural changes, legislative compromises, and key mobilization bills during the 76th Diet session.
subfiles.summary: A State Department memorandum prepared by Schmidt reviewing Ambassador Grew's despatch no. 5496 concerning the 76th Diet session. It details the procedural arrangements following the dissolution of political parties, including the abandonment of interpellations in exchange for the Cabinet withdrawing controversial bills such as the Industrial Organization Control Bill and Election Law Reform Bill. It highlights the passage of major mobilization measures, the extension of Diet members' terms by one year, and persistent criticisms of the Imperial Rule Assistance Association, concluding that the Diet retained sufficient jealousy of its prerogatives to show it had not become a completely totalitarian legislature.
subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs Division Memorandum: Analysis of Despatch No. 5496 on the 76th Diet Session

subfiles.about: Comprehensive report on the organization, legislative proceedings, political compromises, and constitutional role of the 76th session of the Imperial Diet.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew provides an extensive report analyzing the 76th session of the Imperial Diet, which formally closed on March 26, 1941. Operating for the first time without formal political parties, the Diet agreed to abandon plenary interpellations, while Premier Konoe's Cabinet dropped roughly half of its scheduled legislative bills and extended parliamentary terms by one year. The report highlights contentious debates over the budget and organization of the Imperial Rule Assistance Association, notes sidelights such as Konoe's politically convenient illness, and reviews discussions on Oceania and Thailand-Indochina mediation. Grew concludes that while the Diet was compliant, its jealous defense of constitutional prerogatives demonstrated that parliamentary traditions had not been completely extinguished.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 5496: Seventy-Sixth Session of the Japanese Diet

subfiles.about: Reports Japanese press editorials urging the convocation of a special Diet session following the Imperial Conference of July 2, 1941.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports that major Tokyo newspapers (Asahi, Kokumin, Nichi Nichi) were strongly advocating for a special Diet session in August following the July 2 Imperial Conference. The press emphasized the necessity of consolidating national unity, addressing urgent economic issues such as trade adjustment and commodity supplies in the Co-Prosperity Sphere, and defining the government's stance on the German-Soviet war. Editorials argued that an extraordinary session was essential to demonstrate Japan's preparedness and united front both domestically and internationally.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 982: Press Urges Convocation of a Special Diet Session

subfiles.about: Details the opening schedule, agenda, and legislative program of the extraordinary Diet session convened by the Tojo Cabinet in November 1941.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports the convening of an extraordinary Diet session on November 15, 1941, intended to demonstrate the Tojo Cabinet's resolve regarding the East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere and the China affair. The program featured an opening ceremony before the Emperor, ministerial speeches by the Prime Minister, Foreign Minister, and Finance Minister, and interpellations led by Dr. Ogawa on behalf of the Lower House. Major measures scheduled for passage included revisions to the air defense and military service laws, an extraordinary postal law, additional army and navy budgets, and tax increases.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 1806: Convening of Extraordinary Diet Session Under the Tojo Cabinet

subfiles.about: Records FBIS monitored radio reports indicating a postponement of the Diet reconvening scheduled for January 21, 1943, and its connection to Premier Tojo.
subfiles.summary: H. Merrell Benninghoff records information received by phone from Mr. Downs of the Foreign Broadcast Intelligence Service concerning Tokyo broadcasts monitored at Portland, Oregon. The broadcasts indicated that the Diet reconvening scheduled for January 21 had been postponed, with vague indications linking the delay to Premier Tojo personally. Benninghoff notes that historically Diet reconvenings were delayed only by serious internal political crises, suggesting the situation was more serious than mere illness.
subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs Division Memorandum: Postponement of Diet Reconvening

subfiles.about: Reports on Domei news coverage of the 81st Diet's secret sessions, naval victory announcements off Rennell Island, and Premier Tojo's address on Asian independence.
subfiles.from: First Secretary of Embassy, Buenos Aires
subfiles.summary: The American Embassy in Buenos Aires forwards a report based on Domei news dispatches regarding the reconvening of the 81st Diet on January 28, 1943, noting that the Lower House held secret sessions in camera to discuss sensitive budget measures and prevent public dissent. It observes that claims of spectacular naval victories off Rennell Island in the Solomons were likely fabricated to bolster domestic morale during budget debates. The report details the introduction of 88 government bills, a supplemental budget of over 2.3 billion yen, and Premier Tojo's speech urging increased war production while promising future independence to Burma, India, and the Philippines.
subfiles.title: Buenos Aires C.I.O. Report No. 8552: Japanese Eighty-First Diet Reconvenes Mainly to Pass Budget Measures

subfiles.about: Assesses whether the extraordinary Diet session convened by Premier Tojo in June 1943 presaged an imminent Japanese attack on the Soviet Union.
subfiles.summary: H. Merrell Benninghoff evaluates speculation within the United States that the three-day extraordinary Diet session called for June 15, 1943, was intended to whip up sentiment for an impending war against Soviet Russia. Benninghoff refutes this theory, showing that official broadcasts and IRAA meetings were strictly focused on wartime economic controls, production increases, and honoring casualties from Attu Island and Admiral Yamamoto. He notes that diplomatic relations between Moscow and Tokyo remained stable with an operative fisheries agreement and no border disputes, concluding that an attack was improbable without prior public psychological preparation.
subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs Division Memorandum: The Special Session of the Japanese Diet and Soviet-Japanese Relations

subfiles.about: Analyzes the proceedings, executive powers, and legislative output of the 81st Diet session, enclosing a comprehensive list of 89 passed bills.
subfiles.summary: A comprehensive intelligence study prepared by H. Merrell Benninghoff based on FBIS radio monitoring of the 81st Diet session, which ran from December 1942 to March 1943 following a postponement attributed to Premier Tojo's illness. Having been elected through the IRAA recommendation system in May 1942, the Diet acted largely as a compliant body, approving a 39.34 billion yen budget and passing controversial ordinances granting the Premier unprecedented direct control over cabinet ministers and war industries. The memorandum also examines contentious debate over the Special Wartime Criminal Law curbing press freedom, local government administration reforms, and includes an extensive three-page list detailing 89 specific legislative acts passed during the session.
subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs Division Memorandum: The 81st Session of the Japanese Diet (December 1942-March 1943)

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing Chungking Despatch No. 1365 transmitting a memorandum on the significance of the June 1943 extraordinary Diet session.
subfiles.summary: A State Department cross-reference file sheet indexing Despatch No. 1365 dated July 20, 1943, from George Atcheson in Chungking, China (File No. 894.00/1186). The underlying despatch encloses an intelligence memorandum analyzing the political significance of the extraordinary session of the Japanese Diet held in Tokyo from June 16 to 18, 1943.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet on Chungking Despatch No. 1365: Significance of Extraordinary Session of Japanese Diet

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing Moscow Telegram No. 2034 regarding a Soviet press article analyzing the 83rd Extraordinary Session of the Japanese Parliament.
keywords: The War and the Working Class
subfiles.summary: A State Department cross-reference file sheet recording Telegram No. 2034 sent on November 24, 1943, by Ambassador W. Averell Harriman from Moscow (File No. 894.00/1192). The telegram reports on an analytical article by A. Ilin titled 'On the Results of the Eighty-third Extraordinary Session of the Japanese Parliament,' published in the November 15 issue of the Soviet journal The War and the Working Class.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet on Moscow Telegram No. 2034: Soviet Commentary on the 83rd Extraordinary Diet Session

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet (with duplicate copy on page 106) indexing Moscow Telegram No. 3016 on a Japanese Cabinet resolution calling the 85th Extraordinary Diet session.
subfiles.summary: A State Department cross-reference file sheet, present in two identical copies across pages 105 and 106, referencing Telegram No. 3016 dated August 16, 1944, from the American Embassy in Moscow (File No. 861.9111RR/8-1644). The telegram relays Domei news reporting that the Japanese Cabinet adopted a resolution to convene the 85th Extraordinary Session of the Japanese Parliament.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet on Moscow Telegram No. 3016: Resolution Calling 85th Extraordinary Session of Parliament
